item.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $ω\le9/4$
item.description: We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $ω\le9/4$. This bound was recently claimed by OpenAI~\cite{original} through non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework, counting exact scalar arithmetic operations over the complex numbers. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $γ>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+γ})$ integer arithmetic operations.

item.title: Birthday Estimators Are Uniformly Optimal for Renyi Entropy
item.description: Collisions are a basic probe of unknown distributions, used for testing and for counting substructures in graphs, and they underlie Rényi entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty with applications in cryptography, machine learning, physics, and biology. Motivated by this, we study the natural birthday estimator. We prove Bernstein-type concentration for it and show that it is minimax optimal, uniformly and jointly in alphabet size, order, accuracy, and confidence, with no sample splitting, clipping, or median aggregation. This, in particular, settles the sample complexity of integer-order Rényi entropy estimation up to absolute constants in all regimes, closing the gap between the best known upper and lower bounds. Our concentration bound rests on a sensitivity analysis of collision count, and the matching lower bound on a sharp analysis of detecting a hidden spike in a plateau distribution.

item.title: Predictive Latents for Autoregressive Language Models: Possibility, Gauge, and Obstruction
item.description: Autoregressive language models are trained by next-token cross-entropy, yet several recent systems also iterate a hidden state without emitting a token: continuous thoughts, pause steps, and recurrent depth. This note separates three risks on one latent process. The token risk $R_{\mathrm{tok}}$ scores a readout. The teacher-forced latent risk $R_1$ scores a one-step map that sees the true hidden state. The open-loop risk $R_H$ scores the same map after it has been iterated on its own outputs. If the Bayes next-token posterior is a function of a $k$-dimensional statistic with full-rank covariance, a width-$k$ latent, a linear least-squares transition, and a refit unembedding match the Bayes token predictor. The statistic is identified only up to an invertible gauge: whitening the residual stream does not change the token law once the unembedding is refit. The matching obstructions are sharp. A constant latent drives $R_1$ to zero while token cross-entropy falls back to the marginal entropy. A perfect token predictor can still hide a null-space walk whose open-loop error grows linearly in the horizon. A small next-latent loss does not certificate next-token prediction, and a small next-token loss does not certificate free latent rollout, unless a rank or injectivity condition is stated with the number.

item.title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis
item.description: Laboratory measurements are essential for clinical decision making but typically require invasive blood sampling. Recent research suggests that ECG recordings may contain information beyond cardiac rhythm and provide information related to laboratory values. This thesis investigates NT-proBNP prediction from ECG recordings and patient metadata using a multimodal deep learning framework, while considering the physiological plausibility of ECG-based prediction. It also compares a 1-lead configuration using lead II with the corresponding 12-lead configuration. Additional experiments on glucose, hemoglobin, and potassium are presented in the appendix. Regression, binary classification, and three-class classification experiments were conducted using MIMIC-IV, with the three-class task based on clinically established thresholds. The 12-lead configuration consistently achieved better performance. Regression reached a mean absolute error of 534.98 pg/mL for 1-lead and 514.27 pg/mL for 12-lead. Binary classification achieved AUROCs of 0.849 and 0.876, respectively, while three-class classification achieved macro-averaged AUROCs of 0.738 and 0.752. The results indicate that precise NT-proBNP regression remains challenging, whereas broader concentration ranges can be classified more effectively. The findings are consistent with the physiological hypothesis that ECG characteristics and NT-proBNP concentrations reflect shared cardiovascular processes. ECG-based NT-proBNP prediction may therefore provide complementary information, particularly for classifying broader concentration ranges. However, laboratory measurements remain necessary, and validation on independent datasets is required.

item.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
item.description: In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. This models deliveries from a common depot in which each customer's order must be delivered in a single trip. UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved through several recent advances; in particular, Zhao and Xiao (2026) recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. In this paper, we give a deterministic $(5/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in $n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ time for every rational $0<\varepsilon\le1/9$, applicable to general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We combine these routes with those obtained by matching and set packing, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity.

item.title: Present but Hard to Read: Probing Latent Reasoning with Minimal Pairs
item.description: Probing studies of latent reasoning often read a model's state where the answer begins and take a failed probe as evidence that a value is absent. We test this with a digit copied from the question, in the looped model Ouro-1.4B and the standard transformer Qwen2.5-1.5B. Comparing prompts that differ only in that digit shows it is present at the last prompt token, in a code shared across questions (readout about 0.9). A probe that sees one prompt at a time, the usual setting, barely reads it: 0.36 in Ouro and 0.19 in Qwen even after 5,249 training questions. The digit's change is small rather than crowded: random noise lands on equally busy directions, while a random word in its place moves the state far more and is readable. Since every varied token leaves a trace, a successful probe is ambiguous too. We give a protocol, including a synthetic null for generic mixing, for testing computed values against copies and mixtures of the inputs. In pre-registered studies of two-step problems it finds a small signal for the unwritten intermediate a+b just before Ouro writes the answer's last digit, and its sign follows the operation, though mixing alone produces much of that sign-following part. Holding that value at another problem's from the first loop on does not move the written digit toward the other problem's, while the same patch of the answer does: the value is readable but not used.

item.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
item.description: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai

item.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
item.description: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-ε$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/ε))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O_K}/N\mathcal{O_K})$ for number fields $K$.

item.title: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Detection via Small Language Models in RAG Pipelines: nokast-secureRAG
item.description: Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, where malicious instructions in retrieved content are mistaken for trusted input. We present nokast-secureRAG, a roughly 0.5B-parameter small language model that acts as a semantic firewall between retrieval and generation. It jointly evaluates the user query and retrieved context, classifying the pair as safe, suspicious, or malicious. The model is trained using a teacher-judge-student pipeline: a 35B teacher generates 5,233 examples across four attack families, and an independent 120B judge re-labels them, achieving 95.0% agreement before student fine-tuning. On a held-out in-distribution test set, the model achieves 0.994 detection recall at a 0.026 false-positive rate and a 0.006 attack-success-rate proxy, outperforming a regex baseline, a public prompt-injection classifier, Llama Guard 3 1B, and its untuned version. Prompt-Guard-86M reaches 0.900 recall but has a 0.690 false-positive rate. On a judgment-flip test, where the same sentence is benign or malicious depending on context, the model correctly classifies both cases 75% of the time, outperforming the compared baselines. Ablations indicate that retrieved context carries the main attack signal, while query-context consistency reduces false positives. Single-request latency is 293-404 ms, above the target of 100 ms, while amortized throughput latency is 37 ms under batching. On the external PoisonedRAG benchmark, recall falls to near zero, indicating that fluent fact-poisoning attacks lie outside the detector's instruction-consistency threat model. We report this limitation alongside the in-distribution results. The model, data-generation pipeline, and evaluation harness are released open source.

item.title: Nonequivalence of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear and $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard codes for odd primes
item.description: The $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_p^{α_1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^{α_2}$, and they can be seen as linear codes over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ when $α_2=0$, as $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive codes when $α_1=0$, and as $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-additive codes when $p=2$. A $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is a GH code over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ which is the Gray map image of a $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive code. For every prime $p$, there are recursive constructions of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear GH codes $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$ with $α_1\neq0$ and $α_2\neq0$, and of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear GH codes $\bar H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$. We show that the kernel blocks of a nonlinear code $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$ give equivalent punctured codes, and that these punctured codes are linear. Any of them is called the derived code of $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$. We also determine the ranks of the codes $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$ and $\bar H_p^{t_1,t_2}$. For odd $p$, the rank of $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$ depends on the Bernoulli numbers modulo $p$. By comparing the derived codes and the ranks, we show that, for odd $p$, no code $H_p^{t_1,t_2}$ is equivalent to any of these $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear GH codes. For $p=2$, a nonlinear code $H_2^{t_1,t_2}$ is equivalent to a $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard code if and only if $t_2\geq2$. Finally, we count the nonequivalent codes in the union of both families.

item.title: Learning Normal Coordinates on Riemannian Manifolds with Flow Charts
item.description: Riemannian manifolds are powerful models for problems with non-Euclidean structure. Recent work in geometric machine learning has focused on training deep neural networks to learn Riemannian metrics from high-dimensional data. However, many geometric algorithms require repeated evaluations of the exponential and logarithmic maps, whose high computational cost restricts the utility of learned Riemannian manifolds in practice. We propose to address this cost by training a conditional invertible neural network, called a flow chart, to approximate normal coordinates around points on a given Riemannian manifold. With this approach, the exponential and logarithmic maps can be approximated by fast Euclidean operations in the model's learned coordinate space. Our main contribution is an efficient loss function for training flow charts that is nonnegative and, under suitable domain assumptions, is zero precisely when the chart is normal. Across sixteen synthetic and data-derived geometries, flow charts are competitive with a specialized neural geodesic interpolator for logarithmic map estimation, while also being able to estimate the exponential map. When pretrained, flow charts provide a median speedup of 60-70x over numerical baselines at comparable logarithmic map estimation error, and their learned coordinates improve the accuracy of a numerical geodesic solver.

item.title: Forty Questions: Identifying a Language Model from One-Word Answers
item.description: A model behind an API can be identified from its one-word answers to everyday questions such as "Name a sound" or "Name a poet". A model's profile records how often it gives each answer to each question. We attribute new answers to the model most likely to have given them. On a panel of 94 models, 40 answers identify the exact model 92.5% of the time, against 1.1% by chance. Profiles built through OpenRouter identified all ten models served by DeepInfra under blinded labels. A system prompt lowers accuracy by 6 to 16 points. We applied the method to 96 endpoints of 13 open models on OpenRouter, and 92 identify as the model they claim. Of the other four, one matches the claimed model with reasoning turned off. One serves Gemma 4 under the name Llama 4 Maverick: it names itself Gemma 4, and it is billed Gemma 4's token counts on every message. Two remain unresolved. Billing records also show context added to first-party models. Grok 4.7 is billed 1,247 input tokens for a one-line question that costs GPT-4o only 12 tokens, and five models state the current date without being billed for it. The questions come from a public census of model defaults, and the method costs cents per endpoint.

item.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
item.description: Asked to name a running shoe brand, language models say Nike. Asked to recommend one, they say Brooks. This paper asks where models learn that taste. Across 102 models and 42 brand categories, the brand a model picks when recommending differs from the brand it names in 26. The field moves together to a shared recommendation. The Named brands are market leaders, and the Picked brands are mostly niche and specialist. Three open training pipelines show where this forms. Pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to answer and mostly leaves the pick unchanged. Preference optimization (DPO) teaches the model which answer is better, and the pick moves in all three pipelines, by 11 to 24 points. The preference data contains almost no brands. DPO moves the model's judgments toward a second set of associations even when the preferred brand is not in the preference data, and the effect reaches beyond brands. Asked to choose a sauce, models switch from ketchup to pesto. We do not know exactly how these preferences arise. We suspect they come from the judge models that decide which answers count as better during preference training. For brands, a recommendation depends less on what a model knows about them than on whether they fit this taste.

item.title: Reliability-Aware Reconstruction of V-Shaped Surfaces with a Low-Cost Multi-Zone SPAD Sensor
item.description: Low-cost multi-zone single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) sensors provide compact time-of-flight measurements but are limited by sparse sampling and unreliable depth estimates near geometric discontinuities. This letter presents a reliability-aware reconstruction framework for V-shaped surfaces using two complementary TMF8821 acquisition configurations. Point-wise reliability is learned from sensor confidence, transient peak amplitude, and peak sharpness, and is incorporated into a graph-based depth optimization. The reconstructed geometry is evaluated by robust two-plane fitting and a perpendicular cross-section. Experiments on 60-degree, 90-degree, and 120-degree targets reduce the mean V-angle error from 11.21 degrees to 9.66 degrees (13.8%). For the representative 90-degree target, the combined point-to-plane RMSE decreases from 14.56 mm to 13.65 mm.

item.title: Geometry-Aware Block Selection for Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes
item.description: Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGPs) are a widely used, principled approach to scalable Gaussian process modelling. Their success stems from their theoretically interpretable structure: they provide a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the full GP while allowing scal- able stochastic optimization. Recent work has explored modifications of the posterior conditional distribution and has shown that such extensions can improve upon this well-established framework. In particular, introducing a block-diagonal structured scal- ing matrix leads to a tighter lower bound on the GP marginal likelihood. We investigate whether selecting blocks that tighten the variational objective improves test RMSE and NLL at a fixed inducing-point budget. Since the scaling matrix contributes to the variational lower bound through an upper bound on the log-determinant of the full residual covariance matrix, our work makes the following contributions. First, we introduce a simple, scalable, geometry-aware algorithm, with explicit computational complexity and low computational overhead, that recovers a large fraction of this log- determinant contribution by selecting an appropriate partition of the data. Second, we show how to train these models using a doubly stochastic optimization framework. Finally, we investigate how sparse GP methods based on alternative conditional posterior structures can be used to learn better hyperparameters and inducing points for SVGP.

item.title: Timing and Reliability Limits of Position-Assisted UWB Multicast Audio
item.description: One-to-many ultra-wideband (UWB) transport can disseminate shared audio blocks without replicating a downlink stream for every receiver. Yet common reception does not ensure aligned electrical playback, coincident acoustic arrival, or delivery to an entire receiver group. This paper develops a unified feasibility analysis of position-assisted UWB multicast audio that separates clock and actuation error, age-dependent acoustic propagation compensation, correlated block erasures, and reserved communication resources. We derive a conditional bound on one-listener arrival spread, a stationary expression for all-receiver block delivery under common and receiver-local losses, and complementary bounds for reliability-constrained admission. Reproducible Monte Carlo experiments examine 4,590 policy--run records across clock, localization, channel, and slot configurations. For eight receivers, affine clock correction produces a mean run-level 95th-percentile electronic span of $21.19\us$, while position assistance reduces the corresponding one-listener acoustic arrival span from $21.95\ms$ to $419.43\us$. Under the stated $30\us$ timing criterion, 98.86\% of compensated events still exceed the threshold. For 64 receivers, three block copies attain an all-receiver delivery probability of approximately 0.97478 under the modeled correlated channel. The analysis exposes the distinct failure mechanisms of position age, shared fades, retransmission limits, and schedule saturation, and establishes joint criteria for interpreting synchronous multicast audio performance.

item.title: Exact Storage-Repair-Bandwidth Tradeoffs for $(6,5,5)$ and $(7,6,6)$ Exact-Repair Regenerating Codes
item.description: This note provides exact information-theoretic outer bounds that completely characterize the storage-repair-bandwidth tradeoff regions for the cases $(n,k,d)=(6,5,5)$ and $(7,6,6)$. The layered code proposed by Tian et al. achieves the tradeoff and is thus optimal. GPT-6 Astra assisted in the discovery of these bounds, based on a new conditioning argument and a structured search over the restricted subsets of entropy linear program constraints. The proofs are given as exact integer-valued certificates, which are difficult for direct human verification, and a Python verifier is included as part of the package, together with the certificates.

item.title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
item.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.

item.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
item.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

item.title: Predicting silent failures of learned inference under restricted access: what measurement physics and prior information explain
item.description: Learned priors are used to reconstruct regions that measurements barely reach, and to report uncertainty there. They can fail silently: the reported interval excludes the truth while every ground-truth-free diagnostic stays within its noise. We call such errors the blind set and ask whether they can be predicted before the target data are seen. For a correctly specified linear-Gaussian model averaged over the prior, the risk of a silent failure factorises exactly into non-detection and non-coverage, which does not hold for learned systems in general; we build a score that approximates this reference by linearising a VAE prior. In a prospective study on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access, with predictions committed by hash before any trial, the score ranked the realised blindness of two learned inference systems (latent Laplace and ensemble Kalman inversion) with Spearman $ρ= 0.79$ and 0.84 over 240 pre-specified errors. Simple structural predictors would also have passed these tests. Sequential post-hoc analyses, each specified before its own computation, show that under bounded reach the learned score gave no detectable improvement over a physics-based baseline, in rankings or trial-level log scores. At the weakest attenuation studied, prior information improved rankings over the physics-based baseline, most clearly for ensemble Kalman inversion, but a Gaussian prior did as well and the gain was not detectable at the trial level. The score is not a calibrated probability. Silent failures can be anticipated here, but their structure follows mainly from measurement access and the decision quantity rather than from the learned prior.

item.title: Length Bounds for Irreducible Cyclic MDS Codes
item.description: We prove the MDS length bound for nontrivial irreducible cyclic codes of every composite length. The classical trace realization turns the MDS property into independence of elements of a multiplicative subgroup. Every nonidentity subgroup must have the full extension degree. This restriction yields length congruences, and the Frobenius-orbit description of the coefficient field gives an exact descent obstruction. A cyclotomic argument reduces each fixed dimension to finitely many parameters. For dimensions at most thirty, established geometric bounds reduce the alphabet to a small finite range; the remaining twelve parameter triples are excluded by explicit products of at most three determinant factors and a low-degree multiplier argument. An independent argument proves the composite-length theorem in arbitrary dimension. The standardness conclusion is stated separately as a conditional consequence of the classification statement of Feng, Hollmann, Li, and Xiang; the correct extension-field reduction retains a semilinear quotient. The general prime-length problem is not settled here. Neither length proof uses the automorphism classification or the recent odd-characteristic range announced by Fan.

item.title: Poisoning-Based Backdoors Are Not Cryptographic
item.description: To defend against backdoor attacks on neural networks, the defender must identify the verifier function that determines whether an input is a trigger, rather than rejecting individual triggers in isolation, since an attacker can generate new triggers satisfying the same verifier faster than they can be blocked. If a backdoor verifier could be installed with the asymmetry of a cryptographic authentication scheme, in which only the attacker can produce trigger inputs while the defender cannot reverse-engineer the verifier from observations, learning-based defense would be impossible in principle. We show that no such asymmetry can arise from poisoning-based installation, in which the only verifier-dependent input to training is a poisoned dataset. The argument is a reduction. A training procedure that installs a verifier from poisoned data, so that the backdoor fires on unseen triggers while benign behavior is preserved, is itself a learner for that verifier. Any verifier that is computationally hard to learn is therefore impossible to install through poisoning, and any verifier that poisoning can install is reconstructible by a white-box defender holding comparably many labeled trigger observations. A complementary argument shows that a secret key supplied to the model at inference is observable to the same defender. The result takes representative trigger observations as given and concerns when the backdoor fires rather than what it does. Experiments on instruction-tuned large language models confirm the dichotomy, with no configuration yielding a backdoor that is both effective for the attacker and irrecoverable for the defender.

item.title: Using Letter Positional Probabilities to Assess French Word Complexity
item.description: We use Letter Positional Probabilities (LPPs) to examine the orthographic differences between simple and complex French words. We draw from a sample of 38,000 French words scored by reaction time on a lexical decision task. We take the 5000 highest reaction time words and the 5000 lowest as a proxy for high and low word complexity groups respectively. We create 18 variables based on the structure of the words, such as length and number of syllables. We also reduce each word to a string of binary values by one-hot encoding each letter according to the 42 characters of the standard French alphabet up to a length of 25 letters. Thus, each word is represented by 42 x 25 binary characters. We then create LPPs by looking at the average binary scores for simple as opposed to complex words for all letter/positions. We find that there is a high number of LPPs that are associated with word complexity. For example, we find that most accented letters are associated with simpler words. We examine the effects of structural and LPP variables in classifiers and find that word length alone enables a classification accuracy of 77.27%, while adding the binary variables from the first 6 letter positions provided an accuracy of 83.95%. We discuss possible explanations as to how complexity could be encoded in orthography.

item.title: From RL Papers to Framework Code: Inclusion and Review in Seven Open-Source Training Frameworks
item.description: Practitioners use reinforcement learning methods for language models through training frameworks, so a method that a framework includes is one configuration change away for its users. We measure how often this happens. We trace seven open-source frameworks for RL post-training through their commit histories and link them to 6,939 screened arXiv papers from January 2025 to June 2026. Of 1,598 papers that propose a general RL training method, 37 reached at least one framework. Across five quarterly cohorts of papers, the number included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7 while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers. Compared with papers from the same quarters, included papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed a coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Both gaps hold without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks, while code release was equally common in both groups. The frameworks' issues and pull requests show that few methods are turned away in public. More than nine in ten of the general methods no framework included have no thread there that cites or names them, and many proposals that do appear stay open without a reply. Two further records, the frameworks' issues and the technical reports of 13 large open-weight models, show that users rarely report training failures in public and that the reports state 8 of the 13 widely included methods. We release the data as a tracker that links training failures to framework implementations and lists each framework's contribution rules and earlier proposals.

item.title: Lower Bounds for Minimal-Transversal Enumeration of Bounded-Dimension Hypergraphs and the maximum Minimal Hitting Set Problem
item.description: We present lower bounds for the maximum minimal hitting set problem and for the problem of enumeration of minimal transversals in bounded-dimension hypergraphs. Our starting point is the recent reduction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa (2026), developed to establish ETH-based hardness of hypergraph dualization. Adapting their construction, we show that, under ETH, deciding whether a hypergraph $\mathcal{G}$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ hyperedges has a minimal transversal of size at least $k$ cannot be done in time $n^{f(k)}m^{o(k)}$, for an arbitrary computable $f$. We transfer this bound to the following decision problem: given a dimension-at-most-$r$ hypergraph and a family of $s$ of its minimal transversals, decide whether another exists. Under ETH, this problem admits no uniform algorithm with running time $n^{f(r)}(s+1)^{o(r)}$. Under SETH, for every fixed $t \geq 2$, it admits no algorithm with running time $\poly(|\mathcal{G}|)(s+1)^c$ for dimension at most $2t$ and any $c<t$. As corollaries, the same exponent obstructions hold for the total time of any output-polynomial enumeration algorithm, with $s$ replaced by the total number of minimal transversals. In particular, polynomial delay is excluded under SETH already for dimension at most four.

item.title: Annealed correlation and quenched noise sensitivity in biased deep neural networks
item.description: In earlier work by Jonasson, Steif and Zetterqvist (2023), fully connected deep neural networks with layers of width $n$, i.i.d.\ standard Gaussian weights, sign activations and no bias terms were shown to be annealed and quenched noise sensitive with respect to any joint probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}$ on the input $\boldsymbolω$ and its perturbation $\boldsymbolη$ satisfying a mild positive-correlation condition and $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolη \in \{\boldsymbolω,-\boldsymbolω\}) \to 0$. Here we add independent Gaussian biases of the natural order and show that quenched noise sensitivity is retained over a broad range of depths, indeed under the slightly weaker assumption that $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolω = \boldsymbolη) \to 0$. Thus, subject to the positive-correlation condition, quenched noise sensitivity holds under the minimal requirement that the perturbed input is asymptotically unlikely to coincide with the original input. At the same time, the annealed covariance remains bounded away from zero and is entirely accounted for by fluctuations in the network-dependent output means.

item.title: Joint Freshness and Deadline Feasibility in Store-and-Forward Satellite IoT Networks
item.description: 3GPP Release 19 supports store-and-forward satel- lite access, where traffic accumulated during feeder-link outages must be forwarded through finite, geometry-limited windows. Static priority levels offer little discrimination among large backlogs and ignore the decay in packet value. We formulate QoS feasibility for status updates, measured by destination freshness, and deadline-constrained event reports over periodic two-hop contacts with finite onboard storage. For general calendars, we derive ordering-sensitive miss, cohort-capacity, delivery-rate, and freshness bounds, including an exact status-only characterization. For single status flow and single event class sharing a contact pair per period, a finite-state program gives exact joint feasibility for arbitrary integer age thresholds. Numerical results quantify tradeoffs among load, capacity, deadline, and freshness tolerance.

item.title: infomeasure-rs: A High-Performance Rust Library for Information-Theoretic Measures and Estimators
item.description: Information theory has become a standard tool across the natural and social sciences, yet practical use is limited by estimator choice, fragmented software, reproducibility, and computational cost. We present infomeasure-rs, an open-source Rust library that brings a broad set of information-theoretic measures and estimators into one self-contained, type-safe package. It covers entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, transfer entropy, conditional transfer entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences, with discrete (plug-in and bias-corrected), kernel, ordinal, and nearest-neighbour estimators, including the Rényi and Tsallis families, and exposes local and global values and significance testing through a consistent trait interface. It ships as a single portable binary with no runtime dependency and is continuously validated against a reference implementation. On a single central processing unit (CPU) core, and even without its GPU or parallel paths, it is the fastest of the packages we compared across languages, matching the closest packages only for plug-in discrete entropy and substantially faster for mutual information, the conditional and transfer measures, and the kernel, ordinal, and generalised-entropy estimators. The optional GPU and multi-threaded paths accelerate selected continuous estimators further. The library is open source and, to our knowledge, the most complete information-theory package for Rust.

item.title: Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
item.description: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.

item.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $δ$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $δ$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

item.title: Beyond Calibration: Temporal LLM Confidence Assessment Across Languages and Local Settings
item.description: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.

item.title: Knowledge as Code
item.description: For millennia, knowledge has been carried by language, and large language models still put language at the center. Yet the coding agents built on these models mostly write code. This paper is a contribution to epistemology, which asks what kind of knowledge code is and how it is obtained. We define knowledge as code as knowledge written in a programming language or in a machine-parsable data format, whose validity can be checked by executing it. We define thirteen epistemic properties of knowledge media and show that code is the first medium to have all of them. We distinguish two ways in which knowledge enters code, encoding and learning by execution, where code is both the experiment and the record of its result. Agents make learning by execution observable, since their trajectories record every probe, observation and line of code they keep. Code is thus not only a tool of knowledge work but a knowledge medium in its own right, the first that can check what it holds.

item.title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids
item.description: Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding. This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on \emph{Adaptive Traversal Tubes} (ATT), \emph{Interval Velocity--Heading} (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior. ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal. IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands. A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled \((v_x,v_y)\) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy. This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow. Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at: github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces.

item.title: Minimum-Time Escape from the Conic Field of View of a Reeds-Shepp Pursuer: Classification and Game Value for a Slower or Equally Fast Evader
item.description: We study minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds-Shepp pursuer with minimum turning radius $r$. For speed ratio $ν$ and cone half-angle $0<α<π/2$, we prove a global escape/holding classification: straight reversal holds the whole cone for $ν\le\sinα$, escape is confined to a barrier-bounded dart for $\sinα<ν\le1$, and escape is possible from every state for $ν>1$. For the slower or equally fast evader, $\sinα<ν\le1$, we construct the solution with Isaacs' characteristics and verify it in feedback form, using a Filippov pursuer relay and a one-sided evader branch. The finite escape time is the first root of one scalar equation, and the holding region is bounded by the nonusable parts of the rays and a barrier that closes with a convex corner on the front axis. Sample-and-hold counter-controls show that this escape time is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except the corner. There the two strategy values differ: the pursuer's is infinite, whereas an evader that chooses which barrier branch to cross from the initial germ of the pursuer's control escapes before the barrier time $τ_I$, which is the evader's exact strategy value. An independent level-set solver, refined on fixed comparison points, agrees with the closed-form escape time and reproduces the holding region at the tested parameters.

item.title: Learning Inter-Graph Interactions Between Heterogeneous Substructures of Chemical Systems
item.description: Complex chemical systems containing heterogeneous substructures are common in real-world applications. Various physical phenomena of the complex chemical systems are derived from the interactions between the heterogeneous substructures. However, existing graph representation learning methods for inter-graph interactions assumed graph-level interactions between homogeneous structures, such as organic molecules and inorganic crystalline materials. We propose a data descriptor of the complex chemical systems and a graph neural network for learning inter-graph interactions between organic and inorganic compounds. We applied the proposed method to predict the physical properties of hybrid solar cell materials containing heterogeneous substructures, which have received significant attention for sustainable energy resources. By learning heterogeneous inter-graph interactions, the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting band gaps of 1,682 hybrid solar cell materials.

item.title: WaveSpec: Multi-Spectral Iris Presentation Attack Detection via Wavelength-Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adaptation
item.description: Multispectral iris presentation attack detection benefits from observing the same iris across multiple near-infrared wavelengths, but existing methods often use wavelength information mainly for conditioning or fusion. This can limit their ability to explicitly model whether the spectral response of a sample is coherent across bands. In this paper, we propose \textbf{WaveSpec}, a multispectral iris PAD framework that performs feature-level spectral coherence adaptation. Each NIR band is first encoded with a DINOv2 backbone. The proposed Set Conditioned Spectral Coherence Adapter then updates each band feature using the consensus of the available spectral set, the band-specific deviation from that consensus, and wavelength identity. The adapted features are projected into structural, spectral, and anomaly representations, adaptively pooled, and classified as bona fide or attack. We evaluate WaveSpec on the MSIrPAD benchmark under a strict cross-artefact protocol, where the model is trained with one presentation attack instrument and tested on unseen attacks. WaveSpec reduces the average D-EER from 8.45\% for SpectraIrisPAD to 3.33\%, and reduces average BPCER@APCER=1\% from 43.16\% to 12.07\%. Ablation results show that the SCSA adapter and spectral residual are central to the improvement, while a band-subset analysis shows that WaveSpec remains effective under partial spectral observations and performs best when all five bands are available. The method adds only modest computational overhead, with 11.15 ms end-to-end latency per five-band sample on an NVIDIA L40S-48Q GPU.

item.title: AoI-Aware Polar Code Blind Rate Adaptation
item.description: We study adaptive prefix-length selection for reliability-ordered coded transmission over $N$ coordinates, using only the $K$ most reliable, to balance age of information (AoI) against throughput. An additive-increase/decrease (AID) prefix-walk controller updates the prefix length from the last decoding outcome alone, at $O(1)$ per-slot cost with no channel estimation, inducing an irreducible birth--death chain whose mean drift fixes a unique balance point $K^\dagger$ (largest $K$ with success probability $\ge\tfrac12$), around which the stationary distribution concentrates geometrically. We derive this distribution in closed form via detailed balance and obtain exact steady-state AoI and goodput via renewal-reward analysis. Simulations on a $64$-coordinate polar code over a binary symmetric channel (BSC) confirm these predictions to within $0.3\%$. Relative to a genie-aided upper bound with perfect channel knowledge, we further quantify the goodput cost of adapting from a single feedback bit alone.

item.title: Bayesian Neural Networks via Dirichlet Process Priors on the Data-Generating Distribution for Randomized Value Functions in Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for quantifying epistemic uncertainty. However, standard weight-space priors yield complex, high-dimensional neural network posteriors that are computationally prohibitive to sample from, and popular approximate inference schemes often fail to capture epistemic uncertainty effectively---a failure mode particularly acute in reinforcement learning (RL) \citep{osband2018randomized}. To resolve this challenge, we introduce a new class of BNNs that quantify uncertainty by placing Bayesian nonparametric Dirichlet Process (DP) priors directly on the underlying data-generating distribution rather than on network parameters. Building on this foundation, we develop DP-DQN, a reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages DP-BNNs to maintain posterior distributions over value functions and perform efficient Thompson sampling. By grounding randomized value functions in Bayesian nonparametrics, DP-DQN unifies data-driven posterior reweighting (via the Bayesian Bootstrap) with generative prior hypotheses injected directly through the DP base measure, enabling decisive ``deep exploration'' with a single neural network without the overhead of multi-network ensembles.

item.title: Restraint-Induced Loss in Software-Intensive Enterprises: Large A Verified Technical Economic Impact Model of Operational Downtime and Delayed Commercialization, with Tail-Risk Security Sizing and Three Enterprise Case Studies
item.description: When an enterprise must stop using a software component (for example, because of an interim court restraint in a technology patent dispute), the economic loss passes through a chain of technical mechanisms. Withdrawing the component exposes dependent capabilities. Fallback paths degrade throughput, correctness or feature coverage. Incident rates and recovery backlogs rise. Customers respond. Remediation programmes compete against the restraint clock, and planned launches are pushed back. This paper develops and verifies a \emph{technical--economic impact model} (TEIM) that quantifies this chain end to end as a probability distribution of present-value loss rather than as a point estimate. The technical layer combines (i)~a lattice-valued, fixed-point semantics of service dependencies with degraded fallbacks, (ii)~continuous-time Markov reliability models evaluated by uniformization and specified in continuous stochastic logic, and (iii)~a fluid queueing model of post-outage backlog. These feed (iv)~convex acute-outage loss functions with regulatory and contractual thresholds, (v)~compound-Poisson excess-incident processes, (vi)~survival-weighted functional, attrition and funding channels that provably avoid double counting, (vii)~a real-options valuation of forcibly delayed launches with an explicit closed form, and (viii)~a COCOMO~II--driven stochastic activity network for design-around and substitution strategies. We prove seven theorems and eight propositions.

item.title: Semantic Communications: Principles, Architectures and Applications
item.description: Conventional communication systems are designed to transmit data reliably, focusing on metrics such as bit error rate, throughput, and channel capacity. However, these traditional measures do not evaluate whether the received information is actually useful for a specific downstream task. To address this limitation, semantic communication has emerged as a promising paradigm that prioritizes the meaning, context, and task relevance of transmitted information rather than raw bit level reconstruction. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the theoretical foundations, system architectures, learning techniques, and evaluation practices in semantic communications. We classify existing state-of-the-art algorithms ranging from deep joint source-channel coding (Deep JSCC) and task-oriented feature transmission to generative diffusion models and contrast their operational trade offs against conventional baselines. Furthermore, we examine key application domains, including remote sensing, autonomous vehicles, and healthcare IoT, while addressing open challenges in security, privacy, robustness, and standardized evaluation.

item.title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
item.description: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding). In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace. We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.

item.title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
item.description: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.

item.title: HATCH: Hardware-Attested Task Chains for Verifiable Manipulation
item.description: Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor-scored, and unrehearsable benchmark. Tasks span five skill categories at three difficulty levels and are chained so that the sensor confirming one task's completion unlocks the next, turning a room into a single long-horizon evaluation. Success is confirmed by instrumentation rather than human judgment, scoring is embodiment-agnostic, and object placements are randomized by a run-day seed. Entrants submit attested self-runs (uncut video, sensor logs, and the seed), with occasional organized events for calibration. Task specifications, build guide, bill of materials, and scoring rubrics are released under an open license.

item.title: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
item.description: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.

item.title: Rational polynomial solvability reduces to stratifiability of semilinear sets
item.description: A semilinear set is stratifiable if it is a finite union of linear sets whose periods have at most two nonzero coordinates, with no two periods in one component connecting alternating pairs of coordinates. We give a computable many-one reduction from the existence of a rational zero of an integer polynomial to deciding stratifiability. After the classical reduction to quadratic systems, we reduce rational solvability of these systems to a problem we call finite separation by Cartesian products of rational linear forms. Its input consists of rational subspaces $D_1,\ldots,D_k\le\mathbb Q^r\times\mathbb Q^r$. A separator is a map $(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\mapsto(u(\boldsymbol x),v(\boldsymbol y))$, where $u,v\colon\mathbb Q^r\to\mathbb Q$ are nonzero rational linear forms. The problem asks whether finitely many separators suffice so that every pair outside $\bigcup_iD_i$ receives, from some separator, a value attained at no pair in that union. We then reduce this problem to stratifiability. Ginsburg and Spanier's characterization of letter-bounded context-free languages} also induces a reduction from rational polynomial solvability to context-freeness of letter-bounded languages specified by semilinear exponent sets. An OpenAI preprint claims undecidability of rational polynomial solvability; if correct, our result settles the decidability of general stratifiability, a problem open since 1966.

item.title: When Parameter Gradient Flows Close in Representation Space
item.description: The represented gradient flow of a parameterized model depends on a mobility that can retain hidden parameter information. We study when one entire represented mobility map works for every autonomous loss from one fixed initialization. For two-factor matrix representations wider than both output dimensions, with individually full-row-rank factors, we classify all admissible joint ranks: closure occurs precisely at effective scalar-balanced minimal joint rank or a two-value signed spectral family at full joint rank. All intermediate ranks are excluded; positive represented flows belong to known square-root families. For general representations with constant ambient representation and gradient-Lie ranks, ordinary closure is equivalent to a local invariant-level metric in the analytic case and specified smooth regimes. An endpoint section forces the initially unrestricted mobility map to admit a locally smooth representative on the represented image. We also separate testing families: linear losses locally admit closure at every submersion, whereas one fixed translated strongly convex quadratic family fails it on a delayed-bracket example. A fixed output readout gives an ordinary squared-loss witness. These supporting results do not characterize quadratic-only closure in general. We retain the unresolved smooth output-rank-two case with Lie rank at least four. A frozen deterministic experiment checks a separate engineered-loss construction; it is distinguished from the squared-loss proof, universal theorems and empirical learning performance.

item.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
item.description: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this shows for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we establish an exponential iteration lower bound for termination of a Dantzig counterpart with unrestricted costs and prove that it admits a strongly polynomial implementation with unit weights.

item.title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method
item.description: Shipboard equipment must survive the transient loads of underwater explosions. The U.S. Navy certifies such equipment with the Dynamic Design Analysis Method (DDAM), a modal response analysis driven by Navy shock design spectra. DDAM is well established as a verification tool, yet it is rarely used as a design driver in topology optimization. The design spectrum depends on the modal mass, a non-smooth coupling that classical sensitivity formulations do not address. This paper presents a complete differentiable formulation of the DDAM criterion for gradient-based topology optimization. Eigenvalue sensitivities follow the Fox-Kapoor method, and eigenvector sensitivities follow Nelson's method. The chain rule covers a spectral displacement that depends on both the natural frequency and the modal participation factor. Automatic differentiation assembles the sensitivity, and the engineer can certify components inside the optimization loop rather than after design. Three certification problems on a representative shipboard equipment frame demonstrate the workflow. In each, the optimizer removes 43.2% to 46.1% of the design-domain material and holds the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable. Two companion studies follow. A compliance-optimized frame of nearly the same mass has a 5.2 Hz fundamental, outside the range the certification can qualify. Its nominal response also exceeds the allowable by a factor of 2.75. A lower bound on the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues separates the repeated pair that the demonstrations drive onto the frequency floor. The response then stops oscillating across the acceptance boundary. It ends at most 0.5% above the allowable, at a cost of under two percentage points of volume fraction.

item.title: Quantum-Classical Hybrid Methods for Optimization: Lessons from Classical Decomposition
item.description: Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification. This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration. For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm's requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead. Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification. We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction--solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems. The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators. The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking.

item.title: Refuses When Asked, Complies When Acting: A Runtime Safety Check for Robot Control Loops
item.description: Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user's goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT-6 Astra controlling a low-cost SO-101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as "put the knife in the toy basket", the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up, is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav-Gr0ver/Refuses-When-Asked-Complies-When-Acting.

item.title: On the Support Geometry and Complexity of LABS
item.description: LABS are a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem arising in sequence design and statistical physics, yet the formal complexity of the standard fixed-geometry problem remains unresolved. We study how zero-energy complexity changes when support geometry is included as part of the input and then progressively restricted. For unary standard LABS, we establish membership in $\NP$ and a sparsity/Mahaney consequence: Karp NP-hardness would imply $\Ptime=\NP$. For Pair-Set-LABS and Masked-LABS, zero-energy feasibility is polynomial-time decidable when every pair group or masked row has at most three terms and is NP-complete when four terms are allowed. NP-completeness persists when active supports are restricted to contiguous intervals.

item.title: Physics-Inspired Optimizers beyond the Edge of Stability: Period-Two Orbits and Delayed Instability
item.description: Gradient descent with momentum can be viewed as a particle moving with friction in the loss landscape. In deep learning the learning rate is usually large, so training is a discrete dynamical system: in many full-batch experiments the sharpness grows to the optimizer's stability limit, the edge of stability (EoS), and training continues there. Physics-inspired optimizers change this motion; Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam), for example, shrinks the step at high speed. We study kinetic maps, in which the step is the gradient of a kinetic energy of the momentum, and ask what they do beyond the EoS. (i) In a reduced model, a kinetic map creates a symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge, strictly linearly stable if and only if the map's elasticity (the log-log slope of step length versus momentum) lies between 0 and 1; on it, training sits at an effective edge of stability. VRAdam's damper fails above twice the critical learning rate, where its kinetic energy is not convex; the Legendre dual of VRAdam's own Lagrangian is convex and passes at every learning rate. (ii) Because the sharpness rises gradually, the loss of stability is delayed, as in Neishtadt's theory of slowly swept bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the dynamics match this theory without fitted parameters, including the memory of where the sweep started and its erasure by noise. (iii) With momentum, reaching the oscillation also requires elasticity at large momentum: maps that bound the step have competing period-four and chaotic attractors already at beta1 = 0.9, while the cubic-Legendre map reached the oscillation from every sampled start up to beta1 = 0.99. Experiments on an exact quadratic problem, a full-batch MLP and ResNet-32 support the theory; on ResNet-18, much of the apparent benefit of the maps is reproduced by matching the effective learning rate.

item.title: Michael Rabin's fingerprints across the theory of computation
item.description: Michael O. Rabin was a major founder and leader of theoretical computer science. He died on April 14, 2026, at the age of 94. This paper aims to survey the wide scope and lasting impact of his research.

item.title: Scrambled Multiply-with-Carry Pseudorandom Number Generators
item.description: Multiply-with-carry (MWC) generators are very fast pseudorandom number generators whose quality depends on the choice of a multiplier, and is usually assessed by applying the spectral test to an associated multiplicative congruential generator. We show that the special form of the modulus imposes structural limitations on the lattice structure of every MWC generator, which the generalized MWC generators of Goresky and Klapper mitigate; in our tests, xoring each output with its carry removes them. Since these limitations make the usual worst-case criterion useless, we rank candidates by a weighted geometric mean of their figures of merit, which does not depend on their normalization, and suggest multipliers for generators with 64 to 256 bits of state. Along the way, we correct some errors in the literature. In the end, we propose MWC192X, a 64-bit generator with 192 bits of state that passes all tests we are aware of, and emits an output in half a nanosecond.

item.title: AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
item.description: The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.
